issues.description: In Experiment 1, the participant numbers do not sum correctly. The text states 45 started, 5 were excluded from training (leaving 40), but then states 23 were included and 5 were excluded from analysis. This leaves 12 participants unaccounted for (40 - 5 = 35, not 23).
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants... resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: In Experiment 2, Table 4 and the accompanying text are in direct contradiction. The text claims Memory Delay was the only relevant factor (BFincl = 190), but Table 4 shows Memory Delay has a BFincl of 0.064 (strong evidence for the null) and Target Type has a BFincl of 39110.895.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor... (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)... Table 4: Memory Delay | 0.064

issues.description: The authors interpret a Bayes Factor of 2.45 as support for a three-way interaction in Experiment 1. By standard conventions (and the authors' own stated criteria), a BF between 1 and 3 is 'anecdotal' and does not support the alternative hypothesis.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12%...

issues.description: The training task used to screen participants (change detection with rectangles) is fundamentally different from the experimental task (letter identification). Proficiency in detecting orientation changes in bars does not necessarily validate proficiency in short-term memory for alphanumeric characters or mirrored letters.
issues.quote: In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.description: Experiment 2 has an extremely high exclusion rate (92 out of 290 participants, ~32%). This suggests either the task was too difficult, instructions were unclear, or the data is noisy. Such high attrition can lead to selection bias, where only a specific subset of 'high-performing' participants are analyzed.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The threshold for excluding participants (<10 trials per cell) appears arbitrary and is not justified by a power analysis or pre-registered protocol. This is a researcher degree of freedom that can influence the presence or absence of effects.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less)

issues.description: The study relies on 'high confidence' to distinguish illusions from guesses. However, confidence is a subjective metacognitive measure. A participant can be highly confident in a guess (overconfidence) or a misperception that occurred at encoding, which doesn't necessarily prove a 'memory illusion' occurred during the maintenance phase.
issues.quote: Focusing on memory illusions instead of general false memory reports allows a separation of such incorrect but seemingly true memories from memory lapses that are filled in by best guesses

issues.description: The manuscript does not list the specific letters used, only those excluded. Since different letters have different visual complexities and frequencies in language, the lack of a specific stimulus list hinders replication.
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.description: The confidence scale changes from a 2-point scale in Experiment 1 to a 4-point scale in Experiments 2-4. This makes direct comparison of 'high confidence' across experiments difficult, as the psychological threshold for 'certainty' may shift.
issues.quote: participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain) [Exp 1] ... and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4) [Exp 2]

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the 'Short with Interference' condition introduces the second display at the same time as the cue (0.75s), while in the 'Long' condition, the interference occurs at 5s. This confounds the effect of delay with the timing of the interference relative to the probe.
issues.quote: If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition)... In the Long condition, it appeared in isolation... the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset

issues.description: The text for Experiment 4 refers to Figure 5, but the figure provided for that experiment is labeled Figure 6. Furthermore, Experiment 3 also refers to Figure 5.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. [In Experiment 4 results section]

issues.description: The participants are almost exclusively young psychology students (average age ~20-22). This 'WEIRD' sample limits the generalizability of the findings to older populations or those with different levels of literacy/alphabet familiarity.
issues.quote: The remaining 40 participants (28 female; age range 19-30 years, average age 22.2 years)... The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential analysis with a stopping rule based on the Bayes Factor. While BFs are more robust to sequential testing than p-values, stopping exactly when a threshold is crossed without a pre-defined maximum N can still inflate the likelihood of false positives.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor... once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: The dismissal of Fuzzy Trace Theory (FTT) is conceptually weak. The authors argue FTT cannot explain the results because the stimuli are similar, but FTT specifically posits that 'gist' (e.g., the identity of the letter) can override 'verbatim' (the specific orientation) when the verbatim trace decays, which perfectly aligns with their findings.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom. There is no reporting on technical constraints such as screen refresh rates, participant distance from screen, or ambient lighting, all of which are critical for a task involving 250ms visual presentations.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting...

issues.description: Table 1 reports a BFincl of 1.462e+14 for 'Error Type'. While possible with very large effects, such extreme values in a relatively small sample (N=23) often indicate issues with the model specification or the prior distributions used in JASP.
issues.quote: Error Type | 1.462e+14

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the use of fixation color to induce 'transient expectations' is likely too weak to compete with lifelong 'world knowledge' of letters. The failure to find an effect (BF=0.07) may be a design failure rather than evidence that transient expectations don't matter.
issues.quote: If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.description: All tables (1-6) contain repeated header strings (e.g., 'Effects | Effects | P(incl) | P(incl)') which suggests a copy-paste or export error from the statistical software.
issues.quote: Table 1: error rates ANOVA | Table 1: error rates ANOVA | Table 1: error rates ANOVA

issues.description: The authors claim the increase in errors over time proves the error is 'memory-based' and not 'perceptual.' However, in predictive processing (their own framework), perception and memory are integrated. A 'perceptual' error could simply be a very fast 'memory' error of the iconic trace.
issues.quote: This increase in errors over time indicates that the high confidence errors do not (purely) result from incorrect perceptual encoding of the memory display.

issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration for any of the four experiments. Given the high number of exclusions and the sequential testing, pre-registration is vital to ensure the results aren't a product of p-hacking or 'BF-hacking'.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4
